bibl.title: From changing cognitions to changing the context: a dual-route model of behaviour change

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We propose a more general reflective-automatic model (RAM), which postulates that, in addition to cognitive change, interventions can also rely exclusively on contextual change as an alternative route to behaviour change.

span.label: population-wide behaviour change
span.quote: Two very general paradigms for population-wide behaviour change have emerged in recent years – models and interventions that aim to change cognitions (e.g., beliefs and goals), and models that change the context (environment or situation) within which the person acts.

span.label: review
span.quote: In the following section, we review the most influential traditional models of behaviour change in order to demonstrate that such models rely on the reflective cognitive system to bring about behaviour change.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Contextual cues trigger already-existing automatic processes, which produce the action directly, so no belief or goal has to be changed for behaviour to change
span.quote: None of these methods require any change of cognitions, but instead represent aspects of the choice environment, which trigger already existing cognitive processes that, in turn, produce choice of actions beneficial for the individual.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A prime automatically spreads activation to the behaviours, feelings and thoughts historically associated with it, which is why an apparently irrelevant cue can steer action
span.quote: The cue or prime automatically activates behaviours, feelings and thoughts that have a history of association

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: People infer their own attitudes from watching their own (context-driven) behaviour, so an externally cued behaviour change feeds back into cognitive change
span.quote: we form our attitudes, opinions, and other internal states by observing our behaviour and concluding what attitudes must have caused them.

span.label: The paper flags three unresolved conceptual and empirical issues with its own framework.
span.quote: We recognise, of course, that there are still some unresolved conceptual and empirical issues that require further research and we highlight three by way of conclusion.

span.label: RAM explains how people behave far better than it explains how to get them to change; the process-of-change side is undeveloped.
span.quote: The first we develop in detail, but the second is less developed yet.

span.label: Whether SNAP-based interventions produce lasting rather than short-lived change is unsettled.
span.quote: The third issue relates to the sustainability of SNAP-based interventions – i.e. whether behaviour change is only short-term or long-lived.

span.label: The behavioural-economics evidence base transfers imperfectly to population behaviour change: few long-term studies, randomised trials or process studies.
span.quote: In this respect, there are some limitations of applying results of behavioural economics to population behaviour change (e.g., in health) as there are few long terms studies and randomised controlled trials, and few process studies.

span.label: priming
span.quote: Priming activates (cues) knowledge in memory in order to enhance processing of aspects of the choice environment (and to suppress processing of other conceptually unrelated aspects)

span.label: salience
span.quote: The framework is called SNAP, which is an acronym for the following four principles: Salience, Norms, Affect and Priming

span.label: SNAP
span.quote: We also identify four processes: salience, norms, affect, and priming (SNAP), which can bring about behaviour change by relying mainly on the automatic system

span.label: reflective system
span.quote: RAM is a dual-process model which assumes that these two routes rely predominantly on different information processing systems – the reflective system is in charge of changing cognitions and the automatic system responds to changing the context

span.label: automatic system
span.quote: RAM is a dual-process model which assumes that these two routes rely predominantly on different information processing systems – the reflective system is in charge of changing cognitions and the automatic system responds to changing the context

span.label: behaviour change
span.quote: We also identify four processes: salience, norms, affect, and priming (SNAP), which can bring about behaviour change by relying mainly on the automatic system

span.label: context
span.quote: We also propose that salience, norms, affect and priming are SNAP responses cued by the context and working mostly on the automatic system

span.label: priming, in behavioural public policy - a TWO-SIDED operation on attention, and the second side is written into the definition: it enhances processing of some aspects of the choice environment AND SUPPRESSES processing of others. Luoma-aho2019 has the same shape (`leaves out others`); this one narrows the suppression to the conceptually unrelated
span.quote: Priming activates (cues) knowledge in memory in order to enhance processing of aspects of the choice environment (and to suppress processing of other conceptually unrelated aspects)

span.label: priming as ONE OF FOUR - the P of SNAP, placed beside salience, norms and affect rather than defined against framing or anchoring. In this corpus the same word has been a cognitive phenomenon, a media effect, an economic treatment, a property of a mollusc's ganglion, and here a quarter of a policy instrument
span.quote: The framework is called SNAP, which is an acronym for the following four principles: Salience, Norms, Affect and Priming

span.label: the automatic route, as a POLICY claim rather than a psychological one - interventions can rely EXCLUSIVELY on contextual change, which is what detaches behaviour change from belief change and makes the model an instrument rather than a description
span.quote: We propose a more general reflective-automatic model (RAM), which postulates that, in addition to cognitive change, interventions can also rely exclusively on contextual change as an alternative route to behaviour change

span.label: habit, as this paper borrows it - a definition taken whole from Wood, Tam and Witt rather than built: behavioural dispositions to repeat well-practiced actions given recurring circumstances. The recurrence is in the CIRCUMSTANCES, which is what lets a context-changing intervention reach it
span.quote: Habits have been defined as ‗behavioural dispositions to repeat well-practiced actions given recurring circumstances

span.label: builds-on → Bem's (1967) self-perception theory
span.quote: This aspect of RAM incorporates Bem's (1967) self-perception theory, which proposed exactly this – we form our attitudes, opinions, and other internal states by observing our behaviour and concluding what attitudes must have caused them.

span.label: extends → Thaler and Sunstein's (2008) six principles of choice architecture ('nudges')
span.quote: In summary, the set of behaviour change principles included in RAM represent a more general and systematised framework than the six nudges offered by Thaler and Sunstein (2008), which also explains ‗why‘ and ‗how‘ these nudges work.

span.label: extends → the reflective-impulsive model (Strack & Deutsch, 2004)
span.quote: Also, the reflective-impulsive model does not postulate social norms and salience as determinants of behaviour (although topdown effects of attention directed by the impulsive system are discussed).

span.label: builds-on → Webb and Sheeran's (2006) meta-analytic review of intention-change experiments
span.quote: However, Webb and Sheeran (2006) provide evidence that whenever considered, environmental (contextual) change can produce effects comparable to standard interventions, which is based on a systematic review of experimental studies of the impact of changing peoples‘ intentions on subsequent behaviour change.

span.label: reflective system —distinct-from→ automatic system
span.note: differs in: WHICH KIND OF CHANGE EACH RESPONDS TO - the reflective system to changed cognitions, the automatic system to a changed context · strength of the relation: 0.95 — The model's whole architecture in one sentence, and the split is defined by the INTERVENTION each route answers to rather than by properties of the processing.
span.quote: RAM is a dual-process model which assumes that these two routes rely predominantly on different information processing systems – the reflective system is in charge of changing cognitions and the automatic system responds to changing the context

span.label: priming —part-of→ SNAP
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — Placement rather than definition, and it is the paper's actual contribution: priming is put beside salience, norms and affect as a policy lever, not defined against framing or anchoring as in every other record tagged tonight.
span.quote: The framework is called SNAP, which is an acronym for the following four principles: Salience, Norms, Affect and Priming

span.label: salience —part-of→ SNAP
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — The other three principles are nodes on this record for the same reason - the acronym is the unit of the claim, so an edge to it is what makes the membership queryable.
span.quote: The framework is called SNAP, which is an acronym for the following four principles: Salience, Norms, Affect and Priming

span.label: priming —part-of→ automatic system
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — Hedged - `mostly` - and weighted for it. The hedge matters: the paper does not claim the SNAP processes are inaccessible to reflection, only that they do not require it.
span.quote: We also propose that salience, norms, affect and priming are SNAP responses cued by the context and working mostly on the automatic system

span.label: context —causes→ behaviour change
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE PAPER'S THESIS AS AN EDGE, and the load-bearing word is `exclusively`: an intervention may change behaviour without changing any cognition at all. That is what makes this a policy proposal and not only a dual-process model.
span.quote: Two very general paradigms for population-wide behaviour change have emerged in recent years – models and interventions that aim to change cognitions (e.g., beliefs and goals), and models that change the context (environment or situation) within which the person acts

span.label: The paper's model claims behaviour change runs through two routes on two different processing systems: the reflective system changes cognitions, while the automatic system responds to changes in the context.
span.quote: RAM is a dual-process model which assumes that these two routes rely predominantly on different information processing systems – the reflective system is in charge of changing cognitions and the automatic system responds to changing the context.

span.label: The authors name four context-cued processes that work through the automatic system: salience, norms, affect and priming.
span.quote: We also identify four processes: salience, norms, affect, and priming (SNAP), which can bring about behaviour change by relying mainly on the automatic system.

span.label: Across the traditional behaviour-change literature the authors find that every model targets one or more of just three psychological variables: beliefs, goals and habits.
span.quote: they attempt to change one or more of three psychological variables: beliefs, goals, and habits.

span.label: Reviewing cost-effectiveness evidence, the authors conclude that environmental interventions can be substantially more cost-effective than traditional individual behavioural interventions.
span.quote: The really interesting result is that environmental interventions have the potential to be substantially more cost-effective than more tradition behavioural interventions

span.label: Habits are argued to be a barrier to behaviour change rather than a lever for it, because habit change itself still requires reflective goals.
span.quote: In this respect habits more act as constraints on behaviour change, not as mechanisms for behaviour change.

span.label: Salience and norm interventions can change behaviour without any accompanying change in beliefs or attitudes.
span.quote: such cognitive change is not required for salience and norms for have an effect on behaviour.

span.label: Contrary to other dual-process theories, which hold that only reflective/central processing yields durable change, the paper argues that changing the environment alone produces sustained behaviour change.
span.quote: will result in sustained behaviour change without necessitating any change in cognitions.

span.label: The authors claim RAM is the first application of the dual-process paradigm specifically to behaviour-change interventions rather than to persuasion, attitude change or impression formation.
span.quote: first consistent application of the dual-process paradigm specifically to behaviour change interventions.

span.label: RAM adds a feedback path from changed behaviour back to cognitions, which traditional one-directional models (theory of planned behaviour, health belief model) lack.
span.quote: contains a feedback loop from behaviour back to the underlying cognitions, which is not explicitly discussed in traditional methods

span.label: reflective-automatic model (RAM)
span.quote: We propose a more general reflective-automatic model (RAM), which postulates that, in addition to cognitive change, interventions can also rely exclusively on contextual change as an alternative route to behaviour change.

span.label: SNAP
span.quote: The framework is called SNAP, which is an acronym for the following four principles: Salience, Norms, Affect and Priming.

span.label: salience
span.quote: The salience of a stimulus – be it an object, a person, etc. – is its state or quality of standing out relative to neighbouring stimuli.

span.label: social and cultural norms
span.quote: Social and cultural norms are the behavioural expectations, or rules, within a society (or group), which are used by the latter to control for appropriate and inappropriate values, beliefs, attitudes and behaviours (Bicchieri, 2006).

span.label: priming
span.quote: Priming activates (cues) knowledge in memory in order to enhance processing of aspects of the choice environment (and to suppress processing of other conceptually unrelated aspects).

span.label: commitment
span.quote: Commitment is making a choice of a future state of the world that requires some action and imposes some cost otherwise.

span.label: defaults
span.quote: Defaults are options that are assumed as preselected if the individual does not make an active choice of another available alternative.

span.label: 3% ... 30% — share of shoppers who bought jam when 24 flavours were displayed versus when only 6 were displayed, cited as evidence of choice overload
span.quote: Iyengar and Lepper (2000) showed that 3% of consumers bought jam when there were 24 flavours on display whereas 30% did when there were 6 flavours on display (even though 60% sampled the jams in the former and 40% in the latter condition).

span.label: 26% — increase in hotel guests' towel reuse produced by a descriptive-norm sign relative to a standard environmental-protection sign
span.quote: The descriptive-norms message made customers 26% more likely to recycle their towels than those who saw the basic environmental-protection message.

span.label: 28% — drop in teen pregnancy in Kenya after HIV risk information was made salient by partner age group
span.quote: Providing information on the relative risk of HIV infection by partner's age group led to a 28% decrease in teen pregnancy (and 61% decrease in the incidence of pregnancies with older, riskier partners).

span.label: 13% ... 41% — increase in soap use after the toilet and in reported soap use before eating produced by a disgust-based (affect) campaign in Ghana
span.quote: which resulted in a 13% increase in the use of soap after the toilet and 41% increase in reported soap use before eating.

span.label: 22% — reduction in calories per serving expected from replacing a 12-inch plate with a 10-inch plate
span.quote: if the 12 inch plates are reduced to 10 inch plates, this would result in 22% reduction of calories per serving

span.label: .18 — intention-behaviour correlation once only experimental studies are meta-analysed, about 3% of variance in behaviour
span.quote: the estimated intention-behaviour correlation dropped to .18 (i.e., accounting for ~3% of the variance).
